title: Dolce Rosa Cafe Brings Brunch, Pasta and Plenty of Pistachio to Santa Rosa
summary:
Nestled in Santa Rosa’s quiet Rincon Valley, Dolce Rosa Cafe boasts a playful mix of brunch, pasta and espresso drinks.

The post Dolce Rosa Cafe Brings Brunch, Pasta and Plenty of Pistachio to Santa Rosa appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
I’m not here to defend $20 avocado toast. But if you’re going to spend $20 on avocado toast, Santa Rosa’s Dolce Rosa Cafe makes a pretty good case for it.

The brunch staple starts with housemade focaccia drizzled with olive oil, then gets piled with avocado, arugula, burrata, cherry tomatoes, rainbow carrots, crushed pistachios, balsamic pearls, chili crunch and hot honey. Add prosciutto or bacon for $4, because at this point, you might as well see this thing through.

It’s not an enormous portion, but there’s a surprising amount of fine-dining flair packed onto the plate. The balsamic pearls are little bits of food-science sleight of hand, transforming vinegar into glossy beads. The whole thing is so carefully arranged that the toast seems to be angling for a cameo on your Instagram feed.

That, in many ways, is Dolce Rosa’s calling card: small flourishes that take familiar cafe food somewhere a little more interesting.

Tiramisu ricotta pancakes come dotted with rosettes of espresso mascarpone. Beef hash gets a jolt of sun-dried tomato pesto. A pistachio latte arrives with its rim coated in crushed pistachios, like a margarita dressed for dessert.

And brunch is only part of the plan.

More than brunch

In quiet Rincon Valley, Josie Ortega and Martin Chaparro opened Dolce Rosa in July in the former Phyllis’ Giant Burgers space.

They’ve transformed it into a cozy cafe, with an abstract mural of golden roses covering one wall and plants propagating in wine bottles along another. A large espresso machine anchors the semi-open kitchen. Outside, a covered patio offers a pleasant place to linger, provided you don’t mind the occasional truck rumbling along Sonoma Highway.

Ortega and Chaparro also own Chila-killer Cafe in Rohnert Park, known for Mexi-brunch favorites such as chilaquiles, huevos rancheros, churro French toast and tacos rooted in the food and flavors they grew up with.

Given Chila-killer’s success, opening another location might have seemed like the obvious move.

It was the last thing Ortega wanted.

“We decided to never open another Chila-killer,” she said.

Instead, Dolce Rosa draws from another side of what the couple likes to eat: Italian flavors, pasta, sandwiches, brunch dishes and, in no small supply, pistachio.

Beyond brunch, the cafe serves all-day entrees including burgers, sandwiches and mix-and-match pastas with sauces such as hearty Bolognese and tomato with burrata.

“We just want to bring to the community what we love to eat,” Ortega said.

That means making as much as possible from scratch and tinkering until things taste right — including the avocado toast.

Ortega, an avowed avocado-toast devotee, and Chaparro started with a pile of ingredients and kept adding and subtracting until they landed on the combination they wanted. Hot honey came late in the process, but it turned out to be the finishing touch, adding a sweet-spicy edge to all that creamy avocado, crunchy vegetables and crisp focaccia.

It’s also a pretty good summation of Dolce Rosa itself: Start with something familiar. Keep tinkering. And know when to add the hot honey.

Best bets

Tiramisu Ricotta Pancakes, $16: These plate-sized pancakes are good enough on their own, but the espresso-spiked mascarpone and chocolate syrup, finished with a dusting of cocoa, push them firmly into dessert territory. Breakfast, meet tiramisu.

Beef Hash, $24: Soft chunks of roasted beef, rather than the usual shreds, give this classic a more substantial feel. Bell peppers, onion, zucchini and mushrooms mingle with a rich gravy, while two poached eggs and a dollop of spicy tomato pesto add extra punch. It comes with toasted focaccia and hash browns.

Pistachio Latte, $8: The espresso menu runs from a straightforward Americano to elaborate milk-based drinks such as this one, made with housemade pistachio syrup, pistachio cream, whipped cream and crushed pistachios. Also worth a look: the housemade chai latte, golden milk latte and Nutella latte, whose rim is coated in Nutella sauce.

Eggs in Purgatory, $18: Poached eggs sit in a spicy-but-not-too-spicy tomato-garlic sauce, with focaccia alongside for dipping. Warm, filling and nearly impossible not to mop clean.

Dolce Rosa Cafe is at 4910 Sonoma Highway, Suite B, Santa Rosa. 707-931-4625. It is open from 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. daily.

title: Handline in Sebastopol Is Sonoma County Summer on a Plate — And in a Soft-Serve Cone
summary:
After a decade, the west county favorite still draws crowds for fish tacos, oysters, local produce and the chocolate-and-vanilla swirl at its soft-serve window.

The post Handline in Sebastopol Is Sonoma County Summer on a Plate — And in a Soft-Serve Cone appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
There are a suspicious number of entries for Handline restaurant on my credit card statement this summer. They’re all for the same amount: $7.13, the price of a large chocolate-and-vanilla cone from the soft-serve window where I spend far too much time standing.

It has become my after-kayaking reward, hot-day cooldown and “I made it through Monday” consolation. And it is worth every darn cent as I sit in my car licking the brown-and-white Straus soft serve, made with 8% butterfat, before it melts down my hand.

Handline is synonymous with summer in western Sonoma County: beer-battered fish tacos, seasonal sweet-corn esquites, raw oysters, cheeseburgers, cold beer and a sprawling covered patio filled with dogs and sticky-faced children, many of whom are just as devoted to the soft serve.

Parking can be a challenge, but somehow everyone manages. And while the lines can be long, they move quickly.

Located in a former Foster’s Freeze, the restaurant turns 10 this year. Over the past decade, it has become both a Sonoma County destination and a locals’ favorite, largely because it pulls off the rare trick of being casual and genuinely good.

The fast-casual format is simple: Order at the counter, find a table and wait for your food. Several menu items have devoted followings, including oysters, vegetable tostadas, fish and chips, and hand-cut fries.

But the fish tacos are the gravitational center.

“It’s hard to get around it,” said chef-owner Natalie Goble. “I don’t know — it’s a mystery to me — but the tacos get people in the door.”

The tacos start with housemade masa. In a dedicated masa room, corn is nixtamalized, then each tortilla is pressed by hand and cooked on a flat-top grill until it develops brown spots.

Then comes beer-battered rockfish, chipotle aioli, shaved cabbage and avocado. The result is the kind of fish taco that can make an entire meal seem like an afterthought.

Seasonal produce has always been central to the menu. Nearby farms supply nearly all of the vegetables, including butter lettuce, arugula, corn, summer squash, shishito peppers and cherry tomatoes.

Goble, who grew up on a nearby family farm, is particularly committed to just-picked produce and to keeping Handline connected to the farms and fishermen around it.

Seafood is the other anchor. Much of it is sustainably sourced from nearby waters, and the menu makes good use of the catch: grilled oysters with spicy mole and garlic butter, rockfish ceviche, smoked trout and a hearty fisherman’s stew made with the daily catch.

“People want local fish from the coast, and we just bring it a little closer to town,” Goble said.

That sense of place extends to the restaurant itself. The sprawling patio seems designed for a west county summer, with enough room for families, dogs and lingering over another beer.

And then there is the soft-serve window. After fish tacos, oysters and perhaps a cold beer, there is really only one sensible way to finish: a chocolate-and-vanilla swirl.

My credit card statement can confirm.

Fun fact

Handline’s 5-foot fish tank is more than an aquarium. It is an art installation.

How long in business

Handline turns 10 this year.

Most popular dish

Baja-style fish tacos.

The can’t-miss hits

Rosarito’s Ceviche, $19: Clean, simple rockfish ceviche without bells or whistles.

Pollo Correcto Tostada, $18: Shredded chicken, high-class beans and mole on a tostada. Taqueria-good with cheffy, locally sourced ingredients.

Monterey Trout Salad, $22: You will never look at salmon the same way after you’ve tried smoked trout. The pink flesh is less oily, but full of flavor. Served with apples, greens, pickled onions and buttermilk dressing.

Esquites, $10: Not always on the menu, so grab it when it appears. Grilled corn, lime, cilantro, crema and sheep’s milk feta with dried chile. So good.

El Coronado Tacos, $17: Fish tacos. Done right.

Inglewood Burger, $18: Grass-fed beef with Toma fonduta cheese sauce and Thousand Island dressing. Pair it with hand-cut fries with ketchup, chipotle aioli and Thousand Island sauce.

Fish & Chips, $17: One of the better versions in Sonoma County.

The vibe

Casual, open-air and family-friendly, Handline blurs the line between indoor and outdoor dining. Order at the counter, find a picnic table on the patio and let the kids burn off some energy while the tacos arrive. It’s coastal California distilled into a roadhouse: unpretentious, sun-bleached and easy.

In winter, the big windows close, turning the restaurant into a cozier refuge during the darker months. Fish stew season becomes something to look forward to.

The deals

Happy hour runs daily from 3-5 p.m., with a small-bites menu built specifically for that window. It includes oysters, à la carte tacos and snacks that don’t otherwise appear on the regular menu.

It’s an easy way to sample the kitchen without committing to a full meal.

The price

Prices vary widely, from small bites and tacos to larger seafood dishes. Most of the everyday menu falls roughly between $3 and $15, while ceviche, seafood stews and larger platters cost more.

The spot

Handline is at 935 Gravenstein Highway S., Sebastopol; 707-827-3744, handline.com. It is open from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily, with hours extending to 9 p.m. Friday and Saturday during summer.

title: Favorite Restaurants for Middle Eastern Food in Sonoma County
summary:
From casual downtown hangs to elevated restaurants, here are a few favorite spots for hummus, kebab, falafel and more.

The post Favorite Restaurants for Middle Eastern Food in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Oh, hummus. We have done you so wrong.

The staple of Middle Eastern cuisine, made from humble chickpeas, olive oil and tahini, never deserved to become “brownie batter” flavor. But the many ways hummus has entered our everyday lives have also brought us closer to the flavors of Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, Israel, Iran and beyond.

Once all but impossible to find in Sonoma County — or really anywhere outside large cities and pockets of immigrant communities — spices such as saffron, sumac, cinnamon, cumin and turmeric are increasingly common in local cooking. Tzatziki sits next to onion dip at Trader Joe’s. Pitas are as likely to be filled with peanut butter and jelly as falafel.

With several new Middle Eastern restaurants joining the local dining scene, it seemed time to revisit some of our favorite spots for hummus and the many other dishes that make up this vast culinary landscape. And while lumping the rich cuisines of dozens of regions and countries under a single banner is about as silly as saying American food consists only of hamburgers, hot dogs and apple pie, it helps to start with a common thread.

So we’ll plant our flag with hummus and go from there, because everyone loves good hummus. Along with some best bets, each restaurant gets a hummus score from 1 (not great) to 10 (awesome).

And we promise: No brownie batter hummus.

Best bets

Alesta

The recently opened Sebastopol restaurant serves Turkish, Greek, Lebanese and Eastern European flavors filtered through French technique. Don’t miss the flaming saganaki, the crisp branzino or manti, meat-stuffed dumplings with brown butter and yogurt. The mezze platter is outstanding, with small bowls of atom — whipped labneh with brown butter and Turkish peppers — sweet potato hummus, and smoky baba ganoush, served with warm pita, fried olives and pickled vegetables.

Hummus: 100/10

7233 Healdsburg Ave., Sebastopol, 707-329-6533, alestasoco.com

JuJu’s

Michelin-trained chef Jason Pringle has created a Moroccan-style pop-up in Healdsburg that draws inspiration from across the Mediterranean. His Mezze Trio includes three vividly flavored dips — familiar in form, but distinct in execution. The hummus is enriched with roasted garlic and preserved lemon, and finished with a touch of harissa. Baba ganoush carries a subtle smokiness, balanced by caramelized onions, while the muhammara blends roasted red peppers with pomegranate syrup, walnuts and cumin. Served with warm, pillowy fresh pita. Lamb shank tagine is a standout, along with roasted chicken, grilled Caesar salad and branzino with saffron rice. Open 5-9 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday; reservations recommended.

Hummus 1000/10

124 Matheson St., Healdsburg, jujushealdsburg.com

Mazza Kitchen

In a nondescript Petaluma industrial park, tucked behind pots of mint, oregano and basil, Mazza Kitchen is chef Kristina Daya’s love letter to Levantine cooking. Surrounded by breweries, medical offices and contractors, her catering business and newly opened grab-and-go cafe are rooted in warm spices, good olive oil and recipes shaped by family tradition. You’re here for the outstanding roast chicken in Levantine spices and toum, a powerful garlic emulsion with a texture similar to mayonnaise but far more intense. Made from garlic, citric acid, ice and slowly incorporated olive oil, it requires precision. You will never look at dips the same way again.

Hummus: 9

1000 Clegg Court, Petaluma. 707-953-3359, instagram.com/kitchen_mazza

Kalimera Bar & Grill

In 2025, Grill Santa Rosa was notified that it had to leave Santa Rosa Plaza, where it had been serving well-crafted Mediterranean fare since 2021. With support from family and the community, chef-owner Ilyas Kara revived the restaurant at the Brickyard Center, with the same menu but a new name: Kalimera Bar & Grill. Go for the cold mezze plate, a generous sampler of hummus, baba ganoush (roasted eggplant dip), tabbouleh, tzatziki, dolmas, grilled pita and crisp falafel. It’s easily big enough to share.

Hummus: 8

458 B St., Santa Rosa, 707-308-4928, kalimerabarandgrill.com

Spread Kitchen

Opened in 2022 in the former Sonoma Eats location in Boyes Hot Springs, this Lebanese-inspired restaurant from chef-owner Cristina Topham has developed a devoted following. There are plenty of vegan and gluten-free options alongside traditional favorites such as lamb kofta and turmeric chicken in a lavash wrap. The best way to explore is with an assortment of mezzes: quinoa tabbouleh, falafel with green tahini sauce and za’atar fries with toum, an irresistible whipped garlic sauce.

Hummus: 10

18375 Highway 12, Sonoma, 707-721-1256, spreadkitchensonoma.com

Falafel Hut

This longtime San Rafael favorite opened in downtown Santa Rosa, in the former Gerard’s Paella space, in 2021. The falafel is off-the-charts good, and we loved the kibbie — ground lamb and bulgur wheat with a gentle hint of cinnamon. The chicken shawarma was only so-so when the restaurant first opened, with minimal seasoning. These days, it’s excellent, bursting with flavor.

Hummus: 8

701 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-237-7010, falafelhut2.com

Gold standards

Levant

Levant dives deep into the traditional, family-style meals of the Middle East, such as kufta, a ground beef and lamb dish with sliced potatoes, onions and spices, topped with tahini or tomato sauce; lahme, lamb simmered with potatoes; and mansaf, a classic Jordanian dish made with lamb, spiced saffron rice and jameed (fermented yogurt). Cold mezze are a standout, with hummus, creamy labneh, muhammara and more.

Hummus: 9

140 Second St., Suite 100, Petaluma, 707-658-8017, levantpetaluma.co

King Falafel

This hidden gem may be the best falafel spot in Sonoma County. It’s exactly the kind of no-frills eatery that knows what it does best and sticks to it: falafel. Try the King Falafel, with your choice of toppings, including pickles, eggplant, tahini, red shatta, tzatziki and tabbouleh.

Hummus: 7

100 Brown St., Suite 150, Sebastopol, 707-824-4800

Sam’s Mediterranean

You won’t stumble upon this out-of-the-way deli unless you spend a lot of time cruising quiet office parks in search of hole-in-the-wall lunch spots. Thankfully, I do. This charming little place is a Middle Eastern treasure. The panini-style chicken shawarma wraps are a delicious entry point, with gently spiced meat and melted cheese, plus garlic, hot sauces and a Greek salad.

Hummus: 9

613 Martin Ave., Suite 111, Rohnert Park, 707-584-0220, samsmeddeli.com

Real Doner

Here’s another stunner that has stood the test of time. We’re especially fond of the doner wraps — long rolls of lavash filled with sliced meat or kebab. We also love the Pink Sultan, a roasted beet and yogurt dip that is as striking in color as it is in flavor.

Hummus: 10

307 F St., Petaluma, 707-765-9555, realdoner.net

More than Middle Eastern

Fourth Street Delicatessen

This local sandwich shop makes a mean tabbouleh, and it’s the only place I’ve found for mujadara, an addictive combination of lentils and caramelized onions.

Hummus: 8

300 Mendocino Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-573-9832, fourthstreetdeli.com

East West Cafe

The falafel is exceptionally crisp, the beet hummus is ridiculously good, and the chicken shawarma is a go-to

Beet Hummus: 10

557 Summerfield Road, Santa Rosa, 707-546-6142, eastwestcafesantarosa.com

Elevated

Stockhome

The Swedish cuisine here incorporates influences from the Middle Eastern street food common in Sweden. One section of the menu sets aside meatballs and lingonberries for kebabs, pita-wrapped falafel, fattoush salad and saffron rice. The eggplant dip is out of this world, and the grilled halloumi pita is equally impressive.

Hummus: 9

220 Western Ave., Petaluma, 707-981-8511, stockhomepetaluma.com

Pearl

This chef-run restaurant draws on Middle Eastern flavors to create memorable meals. The menu changes, but the picnic plate with tabbouleh, hummus, labneh and fresh pita is essential. We also love the Persian meatball tagine with herbed yogurt, the lamb burger and the shakshuka, a brunch-friendly dish of spiced tomato stew and eggs. Finish with the Moroccan rice pudding, a perfectly perfumed ending.

Hummus: 10

500 First St., Petaluma, 707-559-5187, pearlpetaluma.com

Grossman’s

This Jewish-style deli offers a wide-ranging menu, from latkes to zhug. We love the nuanced falafel, which doesn’t hit your stomach like a bomb; baby artichokes with labneh and sumac; and quinoa tabbouleh. And yes, I’m going to say it again because I eat it so often: the sabich platter, with fried eggplant, falafel, tahini and amba, a sauce made with pickled mangoes.

Hummus: 9

308 Wilson St., Santa Rosa, 707-595-7707, grossmanssr.com

title: Catch a Wave at These Favorite Sonoma County Spots for Water Sports
summary:
From fly fishing on the river to surfing the Sonoma Coast, here are some favorite local water sports to dive into.

The post Catch a Wave at These Favorite Sonoma County Spots for Water Sports appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sonoma County’s verdant vineyards and rolling hills are world renowned, but its rivers, lakes and coast are local treasures. More than just shimmering spectacles for dreamy photo backdrops, the waterways offer an abundance of activities.

From fly fishing on the river to surfing the Sonoma Coast, here are some favorite local water sports to dive into this summer.

Russian River Fly Fishers

Count year-round fly fishing among the many recreational opportunities afforded by Sonoma County’s largest waterway, explains Steve Tubbs, a 35-year board member of the Russian River Fly Fishers.

“In the summertime the Russian River becomes more of a warm-water fishery with bass, pike minnow, and others,” he says. “They can all be caught on flies.”

We’re also blessed with one of just four public fly-fishing casting ponds in the state, located at Galvin Park in Santa Rosa. Russian River Fly Fishers offers free fly-casting instruction from 4:30-7 p.m. every Thursday evening during the summer and fall. Beginners are welcome. rrflyfisher.org

Kayaking/SUPing

Floating is just fine, but sometimes, for a little extra exercise, paddling is preferred. If you’ve got your own kayak or stand-up board, some of the Russian River’s more accessible launch spots include, from east to west: Cloverdale River Park, Healdsburg Veterans Memorial Beach, Steelhead and Sunset beaches in Forestville, and Guerneville River Park.

In addition, several local outfitters make it easy to get on the water, including River’s Edge in Healdsburg, Russian River Paddle Boards in Windsor, Johnson’s Beach in Guerneville, Rubicon Adventures in Forestville, and Burke’s Canoe Trips, which provides rentals and shuttles for a 10-mile paddle through the redwoods.

North Bay Rowing Club

The Petaluma River isn’t really a river: It’s a slough. And once you know the difference, you understand why the 13-mile waterway is a top destination for local rowers. It never runs too fast, never gets too low, and changes direction every six hours (more or less). Conditions are relatively mild, and predictable, all year long, with enough variation to keep things interesting and lots to see along the way.

“Once you get past the [101] freeway bridge, you get out into the countryside quite quickly,” says Nick Honey, president of the Petaluma River-based North Bay Rowing Club. “And there are all kinds of birds and other wildlife. We’ve seen seals. One time I saw a couple of deer swim across the river.”

In addition to organizing youth crew teams, the club also offers adult learn-to-row classes and private lessons. Honey recommends them to anyone who’s interested in being on the river. “You don’t have to have previous experience,” he says. “We’ll show you how to do it.”

On Sept. 6, the club will host its biggest event of the year, the Petaluma River Marathon and Half-Marathon. Now in its 22nd year, the race is open to all people-powered craft, including stand-up paddleboards and kayaks. “People come from all over,” Honey says. “It’s a pretty unique event.” northbayrowing.org

Surfing

Our coast isn’t always rugged and cold. It can be calm and inviting, like the waves at Dillon Beach — just across the county line in Marin — where beginning surfers are still advised to remember that wetsuit. South-facing Doran Beach is also favored by novices, groms, and anyone else seeking relief from northwest winds. Then there’s Salmon Creek, the local test piece.

Ensure you’re ready with the help of Bodega Bay Surf Shack, which provides rentals and instruction for recovering kooks and aspiring rippers — and also offers post-surf munchies with a slice of local surf culture. In Bodega, Northern Light Surf Shop rents surfboards, bodyboards, and wetsuits.

Surf Talk

Grom: Short for grommet. A young (usually under 16) participant in extreme sports, like surfing.

Kook: An inexperienced surfer who lacks basic surf etiquette.

This article was excerpted from our Ultimate Guide to Sonoma County’s Great Outdoors, originally published in the July/August 2026 issue of Sonoma Magazine.

title: Founder of Smog Veil Records Lists Santa Rosa Home for Sale
summary:
Frank Mauceri, founder of indie punk Smog Veil Records, has listed his European-inspired Wine Country home with a pool, gym and game room.

The post Founder of Smog Veil Records Lists Santa Rosa Home for Sale appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The Santa Rosa home of Frank Mauceri — founder of now-defunct Smog Veil Records, known for showcasing the work of Ohio-based underground and punk artists like Pere Ubu — is currently listed for sale. Built by Jon Reiter, known for accenting his Wine Country builds with unique architectural elements, the home has three bedrooms and two-and-a-half bathrooms and sits on 8.5 acres. The asking price is $5,590,000.

The dwelling has tranquil Mediterranean style with terraces and vines climbing the rosy stucco exteriors. It’s decidedly eclectic via Reiter’s signature use of globally sourced elements: French entry doors, Tuscan pine shuttered windows, rosewood interior doors, a Louis XIII hearth and Moroccan scroll vent covers.

A playful mix of color expands on the 3,700-square-foot home’s eclecticism — there are select periwinkle doorframes and rust, blue and ochre walls. Zellige tiles in blue and green contrast with ochre kitchen walls and the seafoam-colored La Cornue range.

Fifteen-inch plaster Rastra-block walls provide added insulation, fire resistance and seismic durability. Floors are cool concrete equipped with radiant heat.

The property offers several places to dine, relax and play. There’s a covered patio with vineyard and valley views, a saltwater pool and spa, the stone-clad studio gym with a fireplace, and a game room with pinball machines and a bowling machine. The home arcade is chic with velvety seating areas cocooned in a deep gray wall color.

For more information on this property at 4296 Savannah Trail in Santa Rosa, contact Holly Bennett, 707-484-4747, 707-935-2288; Sotheby’s International Realty – Wine Country – Sonoma Brokerage, 793 Broadway, Sonoma. 4296savannahtrail.com

title: Award-Winning Photographer Kent Porter Captures Night Skies in All Their Glory
summary:
From sunset to sunrise, the night sky becomes a canvas for stories written in — and among — the stars.

The post Award-Winning Photographer Kent Porter Captures Night Skies in All Their Glory appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
From our earliest years, stories, poems, and lullabies guide our eyes heavenward to wonder and wish upon stars and find comfort in the gentle glow of the moon ushering us into slumber. For photographer Kent Porter, the hushed twinkle of the night skies are a creative and quiet respite from the rigors of covering the news for The Press Democrat.

“When I get really stressed out — even during disasters — I’ll wait around till everyone’s gone home and shoot night pictures,” says Porter.

There are times at twilight when the lunar ascent is so arresting we feel compelled to pull a phone from our pockets and snap some shots, which often confirm that taking a great photo of the heavens is more skill than happenstance. While Porter freely admits there is some luck involved in his evening endeavors, his most captivating images have been earned through years of practice and patience and learned in the self-guided study of astronomy, which provides certain epiphanies.

“The moon is daylight,” he says. “It’s just reflecting the sun. It’s a different shade of daylight.”

Though he receives invitations to set up on private land to capture his images of streaking comets and rippling auroras, Porter prefers to make his photos in public spaces. It’s proof, he says, of what’s available to all of us “with a little bit of effort and a little bit of driving.” The drives take him far from city lights, tramping across fields, scrambling up hills, and leaping over ditches until he finds exactly the right spot where he can feel the firmament’s magic.

“It’s like the stars are sitting on you,” he says. “They look like they’re dropping right on you. Trying to re-create that in a photo is my main goal.”

Knights Valley, October 2019

During the second week of the Kincade Fire, flames swept through Knights Valley, igniting a lone Valley Oak that threw off embers in the breeze. Having passed by it once and noticing how many photographers were making images of the tree, I decided I wasn’t going to make the same photograph. When I passed by it again, only one photographer remained. About a mile down the road, I made a 180. I decided to take a different approach by changing the angle to include Mount St. Helena. I made 10 different frames of the scene, the tenth being the best when the meteorite flashed during the long exposure. Lucky.

Canon R5 camera, 35 mm lens, F4.5 at ISO 800, 12-second exposure

Healdsburg, November 2025

Those who can’t afford a trip to view the Northern Lights keep a close watch on Coronal Mass Ejections, or CMEs, bursts of plasma hurled toward Earth from the sun. The last several years, the sun has been in a solar maximum, raising the possibility Northern Lights could be viewable in the lower 48 states. Tracking the space weather forecast last November, I headed out soon after sunset. As night fell, cloudy skies obstructed the horizon, but I realized the cloud cover wouldn’t dampen the colors. Sensing a near-historic display, I headed from my perch in The Geysers to Dry Creek Road, ending up at Timber Crest Farms with artificial light illuminating the scene. Watching the pillars shimmer across the night sky, I got goosebumps witnessing something so alien and beautiful take shape in the viewfinder.

Canon R5 camera, 35 mm lens, F4.0 at ISO 800, 13-second exposure

Bodega Bay, September 2025

During the fall months, Porter heads to the coast on dark, moonless nights to check out seasonal bioluminescence. As waves crash ashore, the surf turns electric blue, stirring millions of dinoflagellates when a chemical reaction takes place.

“The Milky Way was a plus, and even more unanticipated was the person on the beach with a headlamp, giving the photograph a layered view of the surroundings,” says Porter.

Canon R5 camera, 31 mm lens, F4.0 at ISO 5,000, 15-second exposure

Santa Rosa, July 2025

“Fireworks used to give me fits,” Porter says of film cameras. With those he ended up with more unusable photos than good ones. Digital cameras allow photographers to adjust shutter speeds and F-stops as they go.

“My advice is this: Arrive early, stake out a spot, and stick with it. Then, after realizing the spot you picked out really bites for foreground and maximum burst potential, move in a hurry, trip over several people in the dark, block a few others, and finally pick an area which looks OK through a dark camera and be surprised the first spot was probably much better after all,” says Porter with his dry sense of humor.

Another pro-tip? “The finale never looks good through a camera. Photojournalists don’t stack images, so the final frenzy is almost always too bright with too much smoke.”

Canon R5 camera, 23 mm lens, F10.0 at ISO 100, 30-second exposure

Glen Ellen, December 2024

The Super Cold Moon in December 2024 called for a different location than the other full moon locations Porter uses.

“I had a good understanding of what I wanted in the foreground after a hike I made several years prior at Sonoma Valley Regional Park,” says Porter, who noticed how stark the landscape was with the denuded vegetation on the trees left after the Nuns Fire.

“We don’t have many identifiable landmarks in Sonoma County, such as the Golden Gate or Bay bridges or the Transamerica building. Finding a foreground where the moon is at its largest can be daunting, so I settle for mountains and trees.”

Canon R5, 560 mm lens, F4.0 at ISO 800, 1/320th of a second exposure

The Geysers, August 2020

A dry lightning outbreak hammered Northern California resulting in fires that burned more than 2.5 million acres within a 75-mile radius of Sonoma County. The weather forecast hinted at a lightning bust (a weather phenomenon referring to an electric storm that ignites a large number of wildfires simultaneously), but even seasoned weather forecasters were surprised by the ferocity of the storm.

Being in position early was critical to making a storytelling image. Along with lightning, there were several heat bursts associated with the early morning outbreak. At my position in The Geysers, the temperature spiked at 96 degrees, making the surreal scene more impressive. All five strikes in the image occurred at the same time.

Canon 5D Mark IV camera, 70 mm lens, F4.5 at ISO 100, 20-second exposure

Near The Geysers, October 2024

I did a test shoot of comet C/2023 A3 Tsuchinshan-ATLAS of this scene and failed miserably. I was up too far, wrong lens, wrong exposure, and too late to get any glow of the sunset.

So, I arrived early the next evening, hiked down a steep ravine with two cameras, lenses, and a tripod. I wanted the oak tree in the frame, so it might give a sense of place, and descended deeper down the mountainside. I lined everything up perfectly for a deep vertical image. The only thing I forgot was a headlamp to navigate back up the hill, twisting my ankles in deep cow hoof indentations in the dry, crusty soil. This photograph remains one of my favorite images due to the planning involved.

Canon R5 camera, 100 mm lens, F5.0 at ISO 400, eight-second exposure

Healdsburg, April 2026

I’m always looking to the sky and the clouds to gauge the quality of a sunset. During transition months, when stormy weather and high pressure systems meet, the result is spectacular sunsets, like the one at this varsity baseball game between Analy and Healdsburg high schools. Having a few seconds between innings to get a sunset image with a foreground, the umpire stood in the right place to give me a semblance of composition.

Canon R5 camera, 15 mm lens, F3.2, at ISO 100, 1/100th-second exposure

title: The Camino de Sonoma Offers Hikers a Physical and Spiritual Journey
summary:
The Camino de Sonoma — an epic, six-stage pilgrimage from Sonoma to Fort Ross — becomes a transformational odyssey for intrepid hikers.

The post The Camino de Sonoma Offers Hikers a Physical and Spiritual Journey appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Steven Winter, known to some as Steven the Elder, is the first to mention Billy Goat Hill.

“I thought I was gonna die,” he tells me less than five minutes after I park my car, ready to embark upon my first-ever Camino de Sonoma, a six-stage, 85-mile spiritual walk from the mission in Sonoma to Fort Ross on the coast. “I think there was one part I prayed to die, like take me now,” Winter, a trail volunteer and retired Sonoma State kinesiology professor, remembers thinking during his first Camino de Sonoma experience. “I’ve lived a good 60 years. I do not want to finish this hill.”

I’d heard stories about pilgrims suffering along the ancient Camino de Santiago in Europe, but what exactly was I getting into?

“We don’t do interviews, we do walks,” Camino de Sonoma co-founder Adam Peacocke told me from the beginning. A pastor who followed in his father’s footsteps, both in the pulpit and on the football field, he has a very pragmatic way of building the trail narrative one “intentional step” at a time.

So I committed to walking Stage 1 from Sonoma to Kenwood, and planned to catch up with the group five days later at Stage 6 for the final 13.5-mile climb from Jenner to Fort Ross, which included the infamous Billy Goat Hill.

Soon after meeting Steven the Elder and co-founder Tony “Camino” McCormick, who has completed the circuit so many times (41 and counting) he took on the name of the trail, we gather in a circle in Sonoma Plaza and introduce ourselves. Dino Franklin Jr., a former tribal chairman for the Kashia Band of Pomo Indians and Camino board member, quickly sets the tone. “It’s hard for me to be in this area right here,” he says, admonishing the group of more than 20 bright-eyed, eager hikers.

The bronze Bear Flag Monument towers behind us, and just across the street lies Mission San Francisco Solano. “I know for you guys, you get to see how beautiful this town is. But for me, I’m reminded about what’s in the ground, the blood, the babies, all that was shed for that little place right here to be built,” Franklin says, gesturing toward the whitewashed adobe chapel.

That painfully honest history is something that will come up again and again, in murals, markers, and trailside stories over the next week. Peacocke often describes the Camino as a work of archaeology.

“There’s no way to be honest with it without looking at the impacts of colonization, and looking at what happened to the tribes,” he says.

There is personal pain, here, too. Around the circle, people take turns sharing who they are “keeping in their heart” as they walk. For some, it’s a loved one who died or a parent with Alzheimer’s disease. One person mentions a loyal dog who died, another is walking for a sedentary brother who chooses not to exercise. Franklin teaches us to say “Oh!” in unison after each person shares, a solemn chant of recognition to be repeated hundreds of times over the next six days.

Once we get out on the Camino, strolling through suburbia toward Boyes Hot Springs, different pairings and groups take shape. There’s a mother-son team embarking on a “trip of a lifetime,” as Shelly Howe puts it. A veteran of multiple marathons and Iron Man competitions, she’s a seamstress. Her son Clark, 21, is a welder who fabricates winery signs and is by far the youngest in the group. Sam and Marcie Mills are a married couple from Cloverdale. Longtime friends Jo Arney and Robin Wendlandt flew from Portland. Wendlandt has walked over 1,600 miles along different legs of the Camino de Santiago in Spain.

Another pair of friends, Liz Olsen and Bridget Gray, drove from Sacramento. “I came in cold turkey,” says Olsen, explaining she was “in crisis” when Gray told her, “You need a Camino.”

It sounded therapeutic, like the way someone might say you need an Advil or a shot of whiskey, so Olsen agreed to come. “I don’t know what I’m doing,” she says, “But I’m all in.”

This morning, she’s walking for her black Labrador Gemma, who died in her arms after suffering a heart attack on a hilly trail. Also in her heart is her mother-in-law who died in February.

Other returning pilgrims are dropping in for a stage or two. Franklin Jr. is walking just the first stage, sharing tribal lore along with his personal history of overcoming gang life and drug addiction.

At 69, Olga Barnes has completed the Camino seven times. When the Petaluma resident reaches the tenth, she plans to celebrate with a tattoo of the Camino logo on her leg.

Adelina Aramburo, a retired San Francisco kindergarten teacher, finished stage 6 in February, two months after her husband of 39 years died of leukemia. She says she’s still touched by Peacocke’s words to her on that last day. “Adam said, ‘We prayed for you. We know about your trials.’ It was just very gentle, and it just really opened me up.” She temporarily placed her husband’s memorial card in the chapel at Fort Ross. “He was of Russian descent, a Russian Jew, so it felt like he had come full circle.”

Retired Sebastopol electronics and software engineer John Foley is walking the Camino de Sonoma for the first time. He has traveled all over the world, hiking parts of the Camino de Santiago and taking remote journeys in Papua New Guinea, Africa, and Indonesia. At lunch, he says he feels something powerful taking shape here. “It’s like a living thing—all those people walking the same trail have imbued it with an undeniable energy and you can’t help but tap into that.”

One of the first things to know about the Camino is the terminology: The acronym “OCD” stands for “Obsessive Camino Disorder,” describing the intrepid trekkers who find the experience so invigorating they return many times over. In the beginning, it’s said you’re getting your “Camino legs,” and by the end you’re soaring on “Camino wings.”

“Camino coincidences” crop up in the unlikeliest of moments, like when two people walking on the same day discover they’re both there to commemorate a late parent’s 107th birthday. At the slightest hint of serendipity, pilgrims will say, “The Camino provides” in a zen-like cadence that hangs in the air like “the Dude abides” in the cult film “The Big Lebowski.”

The earliest religious pilgrimages to the Holy Land predate written history, going back to the dawn of organized religion. Every year, spiritual pilgrims retrace well-worn paths all around the world, testing their physical endurance along the Camino de Santiago in Europe, Abraham’s Path in the Middle East, Kumano Kodo in Japan, and the Inca Trail in Peru.

In 2017, during a transitional period of his life, Peacocke set out on a walkabout while on a trip to New Zealand where his wife was born. Learning about the rich history of the land and the Maori people had a profound effect on him. “I went 6,000 miles away from home to get inspired about how we might be able to meaningfully engage the beauty and the story of Sonoma County,” he says.

Back home, he pitched the idea to longtime friend McCormick, known to most these days as “Tony Camino.” More than a decade before, they had founded the nonprofit Hope Works to help people who have been incarcerated find meaningful employment after prison. Born in Texas, McCormick grew up in Southern California where his family often camped with no tents, sleeping under the stars. After more than 30 years as an electrician for Hewlett-Packard, he retired and was ready to walk the earth.

The two began hiking all over Sonoma County, trying to connect a network of trails and stories from Sonoma to Fort Ross, until one day in 2019, they found the missing piece in what is now Stage 6. “We stopped at these two cypress trees, and just looked at each other, and we said, ‘This is tangible,’ McCormick remembers. “And we just started crying. We just got overwhelmed.”

Not long after, 11 pilgrims hiked the first Camino de Sonoma. Today, around 650 people have traveled the route. They expect to hit 100 million steps along the path next year. Pilgrims pay nothing to walk the Camino; the endeavor is funded entirely by donations and guides are volunteers.

There is an element of Christian spirituality to the pilgrimage. Peacocke and McCormick often talk about “walking with intention along the healing path.” Each stage is curated with scripture and inspirational quotes read from a pamphlet they pass out to pilgrims, but they make it clear no one needs to subscribe to their beliefs in order to walk.

Clark Howe, the 21-year-old welder, didn’t grow up going to church and isn’t religious. “It’s never really been my sort of thing,” he says. “But the way that they approach it, it’s not in your face. They say, ‘Here’s what’s important to us, and I think you might take something from it.’”

Volunteer guide Christine Matsumoto-Deveaux is a practicing Buddhist and has seen all walks of life set foot on the trail. “A pilgrim is someone who’s in search of finding what they need at that time in their life, whether it be spirituality or not. That’s actually the beauty of the Camino—we don’t care what faith you are,” she says. “You’re one of us, we’re a family, and everyone is here for a different reason.”

Over the next four days, hikers send texts and photos as they walk through Santa Rosa, Sebastopol, Occidental, and beyond. They stop at a backroad lemonade stand, buying up every ounce of juice much to the surprise of the two young kids running it. Shelly Howe sends photos of the group pouring water from their canteens into Willow Creek near Occidental, a trickle they will reunite with as it flows into the Russian River and the Pacific Ocean at Jenner.

“Fatigue on the feet is real at this point,” she writes after Stage 4. “A lot of hills ahead, but we’ve got this! The group is strong for sure!”

Foley, the retired Sebastopol engineer, was only planning to do Stage 1, but he enjoyed the first day so much, he committed to seeing it through to Fort Ross. On the Sebastopol-Occidental leg, his artist son, Owen Foley, met the group at Analy High School where he painted the Japanese internment camp mural and shared his inspiration and creative process with them. For everyone, it’s the highlight of Stage 4.

By the dawn of day six, the eight pilgrims who have been on the trail since Stage 1 are all exhausted, nursing blisters, sore arches, and stiff muscles. Huddled in the Jenner Visitor’s Center parking lot at daybreak, they’re excited to set out for Fort Ross more than 13 miles up the coast.

Along the trail, Clark Howe found a lucky golf ball he’s been using to massage his feet. His mother, Shelly, has been promoted to the role of guide today, an honor that brings tears to her eyes. Several new faces have joined the group. One, wearing a floppy white sun hat, is John Dickinson. He’s celebrating his 80th birthday, four years after being diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. His devoted wife, Sally Denman, helps him navigate every step. More than a year ago, the longtime Petaluma residents first set foot on the Camino, tackling it stage by stage, and today is their final leg.

As we gather in a circle, Dickinson tells the group how he “appreciates being with you, and talking with you, and learning your stories.” His wife shares how she’s “really grateful our bodies can still do this.”

Everyone chimes “Oh!” in perfect unison, a trail-worn harmony earned over the past five days.

We find a back gate into Jenner Headlands Preserve and wind our way uphill, stopping one-by-one to peek into a shady sanctuary of trees surrounding an outcropping of rocks. A few miles in, Dickinson falls behind. By the time we reach Russian Gulch, he is suffering from heat exhaustion. When the photographer documenting this story arrives, Tony Camino asks if she can give Dickinson a ride to the lunch stop a few miles up the road. The photographer is now “a certified trail angel,” says Matsumoto-Deveaux.

With her husband safe in an air-conditioned car, Denman pushes onward. “The path provided,” she says. “John was offered a ride.”

Next, we navigate a narrow, canopied trail, ringed with poison oak, nicknamed the Hobbit Hole. As it opens into a golden coastal prairie, we arrive at the base of Billy Goat Hill.

Several hundred feet above, truck engines roar along Highway 1 near Sonoma Coast Overlook Park, where we’re headed. Below us, the spell of waves in a blue abyss.

“This is not a race,” Peacocke warns. “So find your pace that works for you.”

This is where Olga Barnes wept uncontrollably the first time she faced the sheer incline; where Steven the Elder wanted to die; and where volunteer Matsumoto-Deveaux repressed the memory of a climb so treacherous that she forgot it existed on her second trek.

Denman digs her hiking boots into the dusty earth. It’s not so much a trail as a series of tiny divots cut into the hillside by deer hooves. She slips, but regains her footing and tells me she and her husband are “Christian and Buddhist, and everything in between.” Between breaths, I ask her why suffering is such an integral part of spirituality around the world. The key to both the Camino and to life, she explains, is “to be open to holding joy and pain in the same moment.”

Stopping to catch our breath at the top, we stumble onto a stakeout, as a pair of state Fish and Wildlife officers hide behind camouflage cover, taking photos of a pair of suspected mussel poachers hauling out heavy bags filled with bivalves, likely well beyond the 10-pound limit. It gives truth to the trail adage, “No two Caminos are ever the same.”

For the next few miles, we teeter on the edge of the narrow highway, guardrails offering the only protection between radiant-hot asphalt and a 300-foot drop. Our guides wave orange flags to warn drivers along the stretch of windy road, which includes crossing a cattle guard, giving new meaning to “walking with intention.” Dickinson, who rejoined the group after lunch, falls behind again, and gets another ride, this time to the finish line.

When we finally arrive at Sandy Cove at Fort Ross, Peacocke is there to high-five every pilgrim at the bottom of the stairs, greeting us with “Welcome to Metini,” an acknowledgment of the original Kashia Pomo village that existed long before the Russians arrived. As the group walks through the replica wooden gate of Fort Ross, it feels like a scene out of “The Amazing Race” reality TV show. Walking up to the chapel, Shelly Howe and her son Clark can’t hold back the tears. “I told myself I wasn’t gonna do this!” he says. His mom is so choked up, she can hardly talk.

Many take off their well-worn shoes and stretch out in the sand. Clark and his father, Darren, who joined the last two stages, splash in the cold Pacific waters. We gather for a closing ceremony, and everyone who completed all six stages receives a ceremonial purple cord. A slow grin spreads across John Dickinson’s face as he receives his symbolic string. It reminds me of something his wife said halfway up Billy Goat Hill: “You need to grab everything in life, because tomorrow is never promised.”

Everyone shares a final thought punctuated by the group’s conclusive, resonant “Oh!” After taking turns ringing the chapel bell, there are refreshments, then they go their separate ways, but not before sharing hugs, phone numbers, and new text chains.

“Let’s do the Camino de Santiago next year!” Robin Wendlandt tells Shelly Howe.

A few days later, Howe sends a text after uploading trail data from her watch. A total of 85.2 miles, 25 hours of walking, and a total elevation gain of 8,353 feet—2,500 of those on the final day. Impressive numbers, to be sure, but they’re only part of the story. “If we let the Camino bring us what we need, we will find it. I did find it,” she writes, confirming one of the mantras repeated along the miles.

The Camino provides.

title: Wylde Provisions Co. Lets Parents Linger While the Kids Run Wild
summary:
Wylde Provisions Co. in Sebastopol gives parents a place to linger over espresso, beer and protein-packed meals while the kids run wild.

content:
I didn’t plan to write about an organic, gluten-free oat pancake served on a paper plate and smeared with peanut-free nut butter. But here I am, stuffing the last sticky bite into my mouth. It’s surprisingly good for something from a kids’ menu.

Small children are screaming, running and jumping around me, which makes sense, considering I’m in their world: a playground in the middle of Sebastopol. Around me is an assortment of millennial parents who look tired but happy to have a place where they can sit in the shade with a proper espresso — or beer — and eat a chef-made tofu soba noodle bowl while their children run wild at Wylde Provisions Co.

All I can think about is how good everything tastes: the yogurt parfait with blueberry coulis, the soba noodles and a giant carnitas sandwich with refried lentils and tomatillo-fish sauce vinaigrette.

At a playground. In Sebastopol. With toddlers everywhere.

Wylde Provisions Co. is one of those “Why didn’t I think of that?” ideas. It comes from firefighter, paramedic and gym owner Urban Anderson and chef Andrew Truong of Terrapin Creek restaurant. The unlikely partners bonded over a shared idea: healthy, protein-forward food that was affordable and portable.

“Food is medicine. What you put into your body is what you’re going to put back into the world,” Anderson said.

Building one bowl at a time

Their first effort was a refrigerator at Anderson’s gym, The Barn Fitness Collective, stocked with chef-made grain bowls packed with macro-friendly ingredients such as curried chicken breast, pickled vegetables, edamame and arugula.

Because the sauce is everything, Truong developed tzatziki yogurt, miso-sesame, red curry-peanut and avocado-lime-cilantro sauces to wake up the bowls.

But as orders came in at a steady clip, they quickly ran out of prep space at Truong’s restaurant. They needed a commissary kitchen and found one at St. Stephen’s Episcopal Church in a space that had previously housed a small church cafe.

With walk-up windows and an outdoor play area, it seemed ideal for both a commissary and a much-needed family-friendly gathering place. Anderson’s son, Wylder — the cafe’s namesake — was the first tester, heading straight for the slide while his father inspected the kitchen.

The cafe has since expanded its offerings to include bigger eats such as meatballs and sandwiches, as well as happy-hour specials like deviled eggs. There’s also coffee, snacks, beer, nonalcoholic bubbles and prebiotic sodas.

Win-win.

New bowls drop Mondays and Thursdays, when service is grab-and-go only. This week’s offering was Berberian Rhapsody — they all have clever names — with Ethiopian-inspired, berbere-spiced chicken or tofu, black lentils, farro, pickled peppers, garlicky collard greens, roasted cauliflower and preserved-lemon vinaigrette. It packs 46 grams of protein into 544 calories.

Past creations have included the Tamariana Grande, with tamari-glazed turkey sausage over udon with edamame, charred zucchini, pickled ginger and cashew-tamari vinaigrette, and the Chipotle Off the Old Block, with chipotle chicken or tofu, quinoa, black beans, corn and greens tossed in avocado-cilantro dressing.

Executive chef Nick Cobarruvias makes the kind of food you can eat every day and feel both good and smug about. There’s plenty of protein and a lot of vegetables, but none of the earnestness that can make “healthy” food feel like homework.

The details

Fridays through Sundays, Wylde Provisions Co. offers an expanded menu featuring sandwiches and happy-hour specials from 4:30-5:30 p.m., along with live music.

Anderson and Truong are now expanding the business through new sales channels, including smart vending machines and corporate delivery.

“Our objective is to create a regional health food brand,” Anderson said.

All ages are welcome, though weekend evenings tend to be the most adult-friendly. The kids’ menu includes chicken nuggets, grilled cheese and, of course, the peanut-free nut butter pancake. Because when it comes to pancakes, we’re all kids at heart.

Wylde Provisions Co. is at 500 Robinson Road, Sebastopol. For more information, visit wyldeprovisions.com/playground-cafe. Weekly bowl drops are announced on Instagram at @wyldeprovisionsco.
